subject: g(0) estimation for bottlenose dolphin aerial surveys

messages.author: 689e7f2b4471c1c7
messages.subject: g(0) estimation for bottlenose dolphin aerial surveys
parts:
We have been conducting line transect aerial surveys for bottlenose
dolphins within a shallow estuary system and are interested in
evaluating g(0) for our study area. Given that the estuary is very
shallow in nature (average depth =3D 1m), we think that availability =

bias
is small since we can see the animals in shallow water and when they are
at the surface. In our study area availability bias can be attributed
to animals being submerged in the deeper dredged channels, where we can
not see to the bottom. We are contemplating utilizing mark-recapture
distance sampling to evaluate availability bias. Specifically we are
interested in using the trial-observer method where the front observer
looks ahead and sets up experiments to see if the back observer sees the
animal as well (both observers would be isolated visually and
acoustically). We believe that the short surfacing interval for these
shallow estuarine animals will allow the front and back observers to
view the same animal during different surfacing cycles. We are
wondering how others have addressed similar concerns of availability
bias in marine mammals with short surfacing durations. We have also
given some thought to utilizing surfacing data (we have some available
for a small number of radio-tagged animals) to address availability
bias, however we feel that this may not be completely applicable since
animals are often "available" for sighting even when submerged. Any
suggestions or advice based on previous experience with mark-recapture
models for line transect surveys would be greatly appreciated.

Thank you for your time.

=20

Wendy

=20

messages.author: 5140016d70f6ba82
messages.subject: Re: g(0) estimation for bottlenose dolphin aerial surveys
parts:
Wendy-

You seem to have a fairly good understanding of the problem. Your
front/back idea will work as long as
you are correct that they time difference is longer than the longest
period of unavailability. If not then
the other ways this has been approached are:
1) using estimate of availability but not just time at surface as you note
2) combined land-based aerial observations (see Laake et al 1997 in JWM,
also ref to Kraus et al)
3) tandem aircraft (Hiby and Lovell Biometrics) and single aircraft with
tandem surveys (Caretta et al MMS)

Also, there is a recent paper that discusses some of these issues.
You'll also find many of the references in ch6 of the Advanced Distance
Sampling book.

Pollock, K. H., Marsh, H. D., Lawler, I. R., and Alldredge, M. W.
(2006). Estimating animal abundance in heterogeneous environments: An
application to aerial surveys for Dugongs. Journal of Wildlife
Management 70, 255-262.

I'll send some of the above papers in a separate email.

regards --jeff
